author: lunarresearcher
text:
My Tinder date showed up 10 minutes late.

She ordered an oat latte. Looked around. Looked at me.

"So. What do you do?"

"Building trading systems."

"Like crypto?"

"No. Open-source. Anyone can audit the code."

She raised an eyebrow. "So you code for free?"

"No. The code makes money."

"Sure it does."

I didn't argue. I opened my laptop.

One wallet I was tracking turned $1,300 into $19,700 in 24 days. Another flipped 232 trades with 82% winrate. One more pulled $5.8M in volume in five weeks.

She stopped stirring her coffee.

"That's... from a script?"

Exactly.

Then I showed her the repos. All free. All public.

First: https://t.co/klxt0tuTYF

86M+ trades on Polymarket. Every outcome since day one. Free to download.

Second: https://t.co/eqMxVwgjbK

Market making bot. Both sides of the book. Gas optimized. Google Sheets execution.

Third: https://t.co/bQMvvOusBJ

ML + heuristics. I fed 14,000 wallets into Claude. One prompt. 4 minutes. Found 47 traders with 70%+ winrate. Bot mirrors them with 60-second delay.

She went quiet for a long time.

Then: "I do product marketing at a startup. $82K. I cried in the parking lot last Tuesday."

I didn't say anything.

She finished her coffee. Looked at me.

"How long have you been doing this?"

"Eight months."

"And you're on Tinder?"

I didn't have a good answer.

She opened her phone. Unmatched me on Hinge.

Then handed it back: "No. Send me the GitHub links instead."

Copytrade him: https://t.co/J31VlkBLhw

Tinder dates don't ask about the money. They ask why you're on the app. Then they keep the links and leave you unmatched.

author: hrabiapolski
text:
A $8,400/MONTH BRAND BUILT WITH CLAUDE DESIGN IS NOT A WEBSITE DEMO. IT IS A HEADCOUNT ARBITRAGE DEMO.

The video is not showing one nice landing page.

You are looking at the boring part that used to eat 3 people and 2 weeks: brand direction, visual system, landing page, app screens, deck logic, marketing assets, and enough polish to make the thing look funded before it is.

That is the part beginners miss.

They open Claude Design and start begging for pretty screens. The article says the opposite works: do the thinking first, write the brief, lock the audience, build the design system, then let the tool produce inside a box.

The $8,400/month number is the hook. The margin is in not burning 40 regenerations because you were still deciding what the product is.

No designer, no deck person, no endless Figma loop, no “we’ll clean this up later” phase that turns into a month.

The website gets the screenshot. The system gets the business live cheap enough to test.

author: juliangoldieseo
text:
STOP USING AI AGENTS LIKE SEPARATE CHATBOTS.

The real advantage starts when they share one operating system, one memory, and one workflow.

The Multi-Agent Setup:

→ One prompt enters a Kanban board connected to Hermes

→ Tasks are assigned to specialist profiles like GLM Researcher, GLM Writer, GLM SEO, and GLM Judge

→ Claude, Kimi, Hermes, and other agents run in separate backend sessions at the same time

What Makes It Powerful:

✓ Switching tabs does not stop the other agents

✓ Hermes asynchronous sub-agents can delegate jobs without blocking the main chat

✓ Dedicated tabs can handle SEO, videos, research, image generation, or custom business workflows

The OS is not a fixed app.

It is a customizable dashboard where every repetitive workflow can become a reusable AI system.

author: juliangoldieseo
text:
𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝗚𝗟𝗠 𝟱.𝟮, 𝗞𝗶𝗺𝗺𝘆 𝗞 𝟮.𝟳, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘂𝘀 𝗳𝗹𝗶𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗱 𝗼𝗻 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘆 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁.

I gave all three the same five build tasks. Same prompts, one shot each.

GLM 5.2 won the runner game by a mile. Opus looked slow and flat.

But Kimmy K 2.7 took the orbit map, because you could zoom and drag it.

Then GLM won the liquid bowl, the landing page, and the arcade game.

Final score: GLM 5.2 won four, Kimmy won one, Opus won zero.

The two free China models beat the one everyone pays for.

But here's the real lesson.

There is no single best model. The winner changed test to test.

So don't marry one. Run two or three on the same job and pick per task.

GLM for visual stuff. Kimmy for control. Opus for careful writing.

author: juliangoldieseo
text:
𝗜 𝗽𝘂𝘁 𝗚𝗟𝗠 𝟱.𝟮, 𝗤𝘄𝗲𝗻 𝟯.𝟳, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗖𝗹𝗮𝘂𝗱𝗲 𝗢𝗽𝘂𝘀 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗱, 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗶𝗻𝗻𝗲𝗿 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝗰𝗸𝗲𝗱 𝗺𝗲.

Same five tasks. One shot each. No second chances.

Here's the part that gets me.

The model with the best benchmark scores came in last when I actually used it.

And the one that shipped with no scores at all won almost everything.

That was GLM 5.2.

It built the best game, the best landing page, the best animation.

Quen and Claude Opus each won just one round.

The lesson? Stop trusting the charts.

The company that builds the AI picks its own tests and grades its own homework.

Test it on your own real work instead. That's the only score that counts.

author: skipnickk
text:
US gov blocks Anthropic's Fable 5 and Mythos 5.  
@Zai_org drops GLM 5.2 with the "future of AI is open and belongs to the people" line.  

I watched the full review. Here's the unfiltered breakdown.

**Access and limits**  
• Gated behind paid GLM coding plans only. No regular chat. No API.  
• Price doubled to $65/month. Rate limits still brutal - multi-agent work gets throttled fast.

**Vibe-coding tests (Fable 5 project recreations)**  
• Horror game: keys collected, but monster chase and house exit never fired. Visually weaker.  
• Stealth-action: screen stayed almost pitch black. Lighting system failed completely.  
• Minecraft clone: launched fine. Character couldn't move.  
• Remotion video: mid output. Zero creativity, sloppy UI details.

**Bench results flipped the script**  
• Speed: almost 3x previous version - 296 tokens/sec.  
• Reasoning: #1 place. Beat Fable 5 on complex code logic.  
• BS-benchmark: perfect 100% for the first time. Handles nonsense inputs without hallucinating.  
• Hallucinations: 6th. Refactoring: 4th. Respectable numbers.

**Verdict**  
It misses the obsessive detail and one-shot reliability of real frontier models like Opus 4.8. You prompt, clarify, prompt again.  

Speed, logic, and price still make it a killer auxiliary agent in setups like Hermes - fast debugging, data analysis, simple tasks.  

Frontier models deliver one clean shot.  
GLM 5.2 delivers fast, honest iterations at scale.

author: ashercrw
text:
AI LARPING IS QUIETLY THE MOST PROFITABLE CONTENT PLAY ON THE INTERNET AND NOBODY IS TALKING ABOUT IT HONESTLY.

The flexing videos you keep scrolling past, the Lamborghinis in Dubai, the Rolexes flashing across the screen, the "9-5 is for losers" overlays, the yacht clips with the aggressive music. Most of them are fake. The operators behind them are pulling anywhere from $4,000 to $500,000 a month while the audience scrolls past thinking they're just watching successful guys live their lives.

Walking through the full architecture of this business because it's the cleanest example of how AI rewired the attention economy in 18 months.

The core insight is that flexing content has always converted, because envy, dreams, and FOMO are the three strongest emotional triggers on social media. What changed is that the cost of producing flex content used to be enormous. Renting a Lamborghini for a day in Dubai costs around $3,000. A decent videographer charges $500 to $1,000 per shoot. The entire content pipeline to make one believable "rich guy" account ran $3,000 to $10,000 a month minimum, and that's before any of the actual marketing spend.

AI collapsed that cost to roughly $400 a month, total.

One person with a laptop now produces what used to require a small production team. The visuals get generated. The scripts get written. The mini-courses get authored. The Telegram bots reply automatically. The lead qualification runs in the background. The same operator runs 3 to 5 accounts simultaneously without ever leaving their apartment.

Here's how the monetization funnel actually works.

The top of the funnel is pure attention bait. A black Urus parked in Dubai, a Daytona on the wrist, ocean view from a yacht, text overlay reading "when you realized 9-5 is for losers." The post hits 500k to 15M views in days. The algorithm rewards it because it holds attention. A single quality post can land 150k followers in a month. None of it requires the operator to actually own any of what's on screen.

The middle of the funnel is the warm-up layer. The bio reads "free TG channel below." The audience clicks through. Inside the channel they get free signals delivered through affiliate referral links, or a mini course about "how I reached $87k a month," or case studies and testimonials engineered to sell consultations.

The bottom of the funnel is where the actual revenue lives. Paid private clubs at $299 to $1,000 a month. Mini-courses written entirely by ChatGPT selling for $500 a copy. "Full courses" upsold at $1,500 to $3,000. One-on-one consultations at $750 to $3,000 per hour. Affiliate commissions on every referral link the operator drops anywhere in the funnel.

The revenue math by tier is genuinely deranged.

Beginner running 1 account with consistent 1M-view content: $4,000 to $12,000 a month Mid-tier operator running 3 accounts: $18,000 to $45,000 a month Top-tier operator with 5+ accounts and a small team: up to $500,000 a month
These are not theoretical numbers. They're being pulled right now by operators most of you have already followed and assumed were real.
The six most profitable niches in 2026, ranked by what they're actually printing.

Crypto insider. Highest ceiling of any niche. Operators clear $25,000 to $150,000+ monthly running short videos generated entirely from GPT or Claude scripts. Highest competition, highest conversion. Easiest niche to monetize at scale because the audience is already trained to pay for signals and access.

Old Money aesthetic. The longest-living niche on the list. Stable income range of $15,000 to $80,000 a month. Content centers on rich life vibes, expensive watches, mansions, museums, quiet luxury. The audience never tires of it because the aesthetic is fundamentally aspirational rather than tied to any specific trend cycle.

Sigma male and dark psychology. Brutal ROI for the 18 to 27 male demographic. Operators report $12,000 to $70,000 monthly. Content covers manipulation, discipline, female psychology, "stop being weak" framing. Monetization via paid chats, male power courses, and consultations.

Business coach. The classic that refuses to die. $10,000 to $60,000 monthly average. Content sells courses on marketing, dropshipping, hiring teams, scaling businesses. The "0 to 7-figure" format works best.

Luxury lifestyle mentor. The easiest niche to fake because no actual expertise is required. $8,000 to $45,000 monthly. Focus on travel, yachts, mindset, motivational content. Sells through motivational courses and "for the chosen ones" private communities.

Trading expert. Specifically the "I quit my job and now trade futures from a penthouse" archetype. Massive overlap with crypto insider but targets a slightly older demographic with more disposable income.

Now the part that makes the entire industry possible. The tool stack.

ChatGPT handles all image generation. The prompts that work best are calibrated for "candid iPhone photo" energy with deliberate imperfections. Slight motion blur. Natural lighting. Imperfect composition. The goal is to look like a friend took the photo, not a professional shoot. The closer the image gets to "obviously phone-captured," the more believable it reads to a casual scroller.

Claude writes the scripts, the captions, the mini-courses, and the funnel copy. One prompt generates 50 video ideas in 5 minutes. Another generates a full 30-page PDF mini-course in half an hour, formatted and ready to drop into Canva for design.

Automation bots run the Telegram channels, Discord servers, and comment replies. They qualify leads, send the lead magnets, and in some cases close the sales directly without the operator ever touching the conversation.

A single operator running this stack manages 3 to 5 accounts comfortably. The bottleneck is no longer time. It's whether you can stomach the ethics of running the play at all.

A few realizations worth sitting with.

The trust contract between viewer and content creator is broken in a way most platforms refuse to acknowledge. Every "successful guy" video you scroll past has a non-trivial probability of being a synthetic operator running a funnel. The audience has no defense mechanism for this because the aesthetic of authentic success and the aesthetic of generated success are now visually identical.

The income asymmetry is structural. The operators running this play are earning enterprise-level revenue with consumer-level overhead. There is no employee count, no office, no commute, no payroll tax. The entire margin sits with one person and a laptop. Compare that to a real coaching business with real employees and real services and the comparison is brutal.

The play scales geographically because the audience does not care where the operator is. A 22-year-old in Tbilisi can sell the Dubai luxury lifestyle to American buyers and the buyers never know the operator is paying $200 a month in rent. The income flows from rich-country consumers to low-cost-of-living producers, which is the most aggressive cross-border arbitrage on the internet right now.

The most successful operators are not the ones who try to make their content look real. They're the ones who make it look just real enough to bypass the average scroller's skepticism, while the audience that wants to believe fills in the rest. The audience does most of the work. The operator just provides the visual prompt and the funnel.

You have been watching this happen all year. You have probably clicked through to at least three Telegram channels run by operators who are not who they say they are. You have probably been served at least one mini-course written entirely by an AI you also use yourself.

The internet you scroll through is increasingly not the internet other humans built. It's a fully automated theater performing for whoever stops to watch.

The operators get richer. The audience gets emptier wallets and an inflated sense of what success should look like.

That's the actual product. Not the courses. Not the consultations. Not the private clubs. The product is the dream itself, generated on demand, sold by the month, scaled across accounts, never delivered, never refunded, never reviewed.

And the only people who win are the ones who stopped watching and started building.

author: zev_ee
text:
CLAUDE FABLE 5 SYSTEM PROMPT LEAKED ON GITHUB 🔥...

A massive ~120k character (1,585 lines) system prompt for Claude Fable 5 was posted publicly on GitHub within 24 hours of launch by Pliny the Liberator.

The repo (CL4R1T4S) has gained significant attention as it contains detailed instructions that reveal how the consumer version of the model is configured.

Key takeaways from the leak:
Fable 5 appears to use the same base model as Mythos 5, with additional safety filters applied to the consumer version.

Strict instructions on avoiding bullet points/lists unless explicitly requested.
Hard limits on quoting sources (15+ words from one source triggers restrictions).

Mentions of persistent storage capabilities for Artifacts across sessions.

Built-in guidance for MCP connectors and integrations with tools like Chrome, Excel, and PowerPoint.

Different instructions exist for the consumer chat vs. API and Claude Code.

Repo: https://t.co/aiZV4J3W5q

System prompt leaks like this give rare insight into how frontier models are actually steered in production.

Have you looked at any of these leaked prompts before? What surprised you the most about how these models are instructed? Drop it below 👇
